title: OpenAI launches 'Businesses in ChatGPT' beta with claimable profiles and merchant agents
subtitle: Companies can now verify a Business Hub profile and deploy an OpenAI-hosted Business Agent that answers customer questions and transacts inside ChatGPT. Launch is scoped to eligible US ecommerce and online-service merchants, with ads as a planned revenue channel.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: OpenAI opened a beta it is calling 'Businesses in ChatGPT' on November 10, split into two products. The first is a Business Hub, where companies claim a verified profile, maintain product feeds and contact details, and see aggregated engagement data on how ChatGPT users interact with them. The second is Business Agents — OpenAI-hosted, clearly labeled chat agents that answer customer questions inside the ChatGPT interface. Business Agents are available first to eligible US ecommerce and online-service merchants; Business Hub claiming has broader geographic eligibility. Existing enterprise customers and advertisers can claim through their OpenAI representative. OpenAI says it does not share user conversations or Business Agent chats with the merchant, and that paying for ChatGPT Ads does not change how often a business gets recommended.

This is the agent-economy counterpart to Google's search snippet, and it is structurally more aggressive. The Business Hub is a canonical record OpenAI controls — not a third-party website scraped on the fly — and Business Agents are a managed runtime where the merchant does not bring its own model. Digiday confirmed the current beta does not permit bring-your-own-agent integration. That matters because it makes the ChatGPT product surface a two-sided marketplace with OpenAI as the sole broker, in the same architectural position Apple holds for iOS app distribution. Advertising becomes the obvious second revenue stream after inference, and the privacy fencing between users and merchants keeps the first-party relationship with the user intact.

Industry reaction splits along two lines. Companies that already rely on direct-to-consumer web traffic see this as a near-term risk to conversion attribution and to the terms on which they appear inside the LLM interface. Payment processors, marketplaces, and verticalized agent startups see it as a floor — anything they build has to beat an OpenAI-hosted default that is already distributed to 800 million weekly users. The same dynamic is playing out at Anthropic with Claude's Plaid integration (launched November 7) and at Google with Gemini commerce workflows. Different mechanics, same architectural claim: the LLM vendor owns the customer, and the merchant plugs in through a managed interface.

A takeaway for learners: if you are building a consumer-facing product, start treating 'how does this appear inside ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini' as a distribution question on par with search and app-store placement. The verified-profile step is low-cost to complete and sets the ground truth the model will cite. If you are studying platforms, note how fast OpenAI has moved from a chat product to a two-sided marketplace — a transition that took Google six years and Apple two.
